{{Short description|Law in algebra}}
{{about|the algebraic identity|relation between chemical material and attenuation of light|Beer–Lambert law}}
In [[algebra]], the '''absorption law''' or '''absorption identity''' is an [[Identity (mathematics)|identity]] linking a pair of [[binary operations]].

Two binary operations, ¤ and ⁂, are said to be connected by the absorption law if:

:''a'' ¤ (''a'' ⁂ ''b'') = ''a'' ⁂ (''a'' ¤ ''b'') = ''a''.

== Examples ==

=== Lattices ===

A [[Set (mathematics)|set]] equipped with two [[commutative]] and [[associative]] binary operations <math>\scriptstyle \lor</math> ("join") and <math>\scriptstyle \land</math> ("meet") that are connected by the absorption law is called a [[Lattice (order)#Lattices as algebraic structures|lattice]]; in this case, both operations are necessarily [[Idempotence|idempotent]] (i.e. ''a'' <math>\scriptstyle \lor</math> ''a'' = ''a'' and ''a'' <math>\scriptstyle \land</math> ''a'' = ''a'').

Examples of lattices include [[Heyting algebra]]s and [[Boolean algebra (structure)|Boolean algebras]],<ref>See [[Boolean algebra (structure)#Axiomatics]] for a proof of the absorption laws from the distributivity, identity, and boundary laws.</ref> in particular sets of sets with ''[[Union (set theory)|union]]'' (∪) and ''[[Intersection (set theory)|intersection]]'' (∩) operators,  [[List of order structures in mathematics|ordered sets]] with [[Maximal element|''min'' and ''max'']] operations and [[integer]]s with [[least common multiple]] and [[greatest common divisor]].

=== Logic ===

In [[classical logic]], and in particular [[Boolean algebra (logic)|Boolean algebra]], the operations [[Logical disjunction|OR]] and [[Logical conjunction|AND]], which are also denoted by <math>\scriptstyle \lor</math> and <math>\scriptstyle \land</math>, satisfy the lattice axioms, including the absorption law. The same is true for [[intuitionistic logic]].

=== Non-examples ===

The absorption law does not hold in many other algebraic structures, such as [[commutative ring]]s, ''e.g.'' the [[Field (mathematics)|field]] of [[real number]]s, [[relevance logic]]s, [[linear logic]]s, and [[substructural logic]]s. In the last case, there is no [[one-to-one correspondence]] between the [[free variable]]s of the defining pair of identities.
